subject: PrivateNet tail-latency gates & test window
messages:
From: Tom Lin <tom.lin@riverside.ai>

Cc: ops@riverside.ai
Date: 2027-08-02T15:10:00Z
Subject: PrivateNet tail-latency gates & test window

Thanks for the call today — quick recap from our side and a couple of clarifying questions so we can coordinate a lab window.

TL;DR: Riverside expects p95 request-to-response < 120 ms and p99 (tail) < 260 ms for 1:1 inference traffic (small prompt sizes, ~200 tokens). For streaming transcriptions we need sustained 200 concurrent streams with no single-chunk latency spikes above 300 ms. We run through a VPC peering + NAT egress path to our customer-managed transit; that path adds ~20-40 ms typical, but we see jitter during burst.

Open items we need help validating in the private deployment:
- Where should we measure the end-to-end latency target (Redwood LB -> GPU vs Redwoods edge node -> GPU)?
- Any recommended MTU or TCP tuning for the VPN/peering path to avoid fragmentation for streaming audio chunks?
- Can Redwood produce a short synthetic load plan that exercises both concurrent streaming and high request-per-second bursts (we can run client and capture tcpdump/pcap)?

I'll attach a short summary of our production tail samples and an ops contact. Prefer a 3-hour test window next week (Aug 5 or 6) during your Pacific morning.

Thanks,
Tom Lin
Platform Eng, Riverside AI
ops@riverside.ai

From: Priya Natarajan <priya_natarajan@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: PrivateNet tail-latency gates & test window

Tom — appreciated the clear targets. Recap and proposed plan from Redwood below. Please confirm the test window that works for your ops team.

Summary of Redwood understanding and measurement points:
- Measurement points: we will capture timestamps at (A) Redwood public LB / peer-facing router, (B) Private node ingress (Redwood side of peering), and (C) GPU worker process (token generation start). For contractual SLOs we recommend point B -> C (Redwood-controlled network plus host latency). For your internal acceptance you can compare A -> C to include your transit.
- Targets: agree to validate p95 < 120 ms (B->C) and p99 < 260 ms (B->C) for 1:1 non-streaming. For streaming, validate sustained 200 concurrent streams with 95th per-chunk latency < 180 ms and 99th < 300 ms.
- Concurrency/throughput: we expect these tests to exercise up to 600 rps burst for batch requests and 200 simultaneous RT streams; please confirm average payload sizes (you mentioned ~200 tokens; also give average chunk size in bytes for streaming).

Proposed test plan (high level):
1) Baseline: 15 min low-volume run to collect RTT and packet loss baseline (we will capture pcap).
2) Non-streaming bursts: step load 50 -> 200 -> 600 rps in 10-min blocks; measure p50/p95/p99 across points B and C.
3) Streaming: ramp to 200 concurrent streams, maintain for 20 minutes, then inject a sudden 2x burst for 2 minutes to observe tail behavior and KV cache warm/cold transitions.
4) Failover/fallback: simulate an instance eviction to validate automatic fallback to secondary private pool and how it affects tail.

Karthik will provide the exact synthetic client and sigterm behavior. We can run Aug 5 09:00-12:00 PT or Aug 6 09:00-12:00 PT. I've attached a draft test plan and a tiny sample pcap for reference.

Action items for Riverside: confirm streaming chunk size and preferred test date/time.

Regards,
Priya Natarajan
Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: PrivateNet tail-latency gates & test window

Adding technical detail — this is the test harness and the internal latency budget we recommend for the private deployment.

Quick notes: we intentionally separate network egress traversal jitter from host scheduling. For private deployments the typical hop layout is: customer-transit -> peering router -> Redwood edge node -> LB -> worker host (container) -> local GPU process. The part we control most tightly is edge node -> worker.

Internal latency budget (Redwood-side):
- Edge node routing + TLS termination: target 10-25 ms median, p95 < 40 ms
- LB + request routing to host: target 8-18 ms median, p95 < 35 ms
- Host queuing + GPU kernel launch + first-token generation: target 20-60 ms median, p95 < 120 ms
- Combined Redwood B->C target: p95 < 120 ms, p99 < 260 ms (matches Priya's note)

Networking tuning notes:
- MTU: if you are terminating VPN over AWS Transit Gateway / on-prem transit, please ensure MTU >= 1400 to avoid fragmentation for ~1kb streaming chunks.
- TCP: enable TCP_NODELAY on client side; use BBR v2 where possible for throughput stability.
- Egress: we prefer BGP peering to avoid asymmetric NAT where possible; if NAT is required, ensure sticky NAT mappings for long-lived streams.

Test harness: we'll provide a containerized client that supports both RPC style requests and gRPC streaming with configurable chunk size. It will produce Prometheus metrics and a combined pcap capture hook. After the run we will share pcap + Prometheus scrape for both sides.

I'll attach the client run command and the Prometheus job definitions to the test-plan PDF.

-Karthik
Senior SRE, Redwood Inference

From: Tom Lin <tom.lin@riverside.ai>

Thanks Karthik — that level of granularity is perfect. Quick answers from our side:
- Streaming chunk sizes: typical chunks are 6-8KB for encoded audio frames, but we can reduce to 1KB for the test if that helps isolate per-chunk latency.
- We'll prefer BGP peering but currently run via a managed transit that sits behind a NAT gateway. Team can set up a temporary overlay to preserve source IP if needed.
- Confirmed production concurrency: sustained 200 streams with occasional peaks to 280 for up to 90s. We can reproduce that in the lab.

We prefer Aug 5 09:00-12:00 PT. Procurement is cc'd — if Redwood needs a short PoA or non-prod access window let procurement know and we'll expedite.

Also — one ask: can Redwood include a quick run of quantized model variant to see if there's any delta on tail latency vs full-precision model? We understand quantization can change kernel paths and scheduling.

Tom
Tom Lin
Platform Eng, Riverside AI
